record.abstract: Lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG3) protein is a key immune inhibitory checkpoint receptor that suppresses T cell activation, proliferation and effector functions to maintain immune homeostasis and tolerance. In persistent pathological settings, chronic T cell receptor (TCR) signalling, together with sustained LAG3 signalling and other inhibitory receptor signalling, drives T cell dysfunction, highlighting LAG3 as a promising therapeutic target. However, more than 30 years after its discovery, the fundamental mechanisms governing LAG3 signalling and function remain incompletely defined. Elucidating LAG3 downstream signalling pathways and the mechanisms of action of LAG3-blocking antibodies is essential for identifying optimal clinical indications, developing predictive biomarkers, designing more effective LAG3-targeted therapeutics and maximizing clinical efficacy. Recent advances have revealed key molecular mechanisms, including constitutive tonic signalling, ligand-induced ubiquitination-dependent signalling switches and LAG3-TCR proximity-mediated suppression. In this Review, we comprehensively examine LAG3 signalling mechanisms, synthesize current understanding of its functional effect on T cells, discuss emerging therapeutics and their mechanisms of action, and evaluate biomarker strategies for patient selection. We conclude by highlighting key challenges and outlining future directions for LAG3-targeted immunotherapy in oncology and autoimmune disease.

record.abstract: Peyer's patches (PPs) in the intestinal mucosa coordinate antibody responses to luminal microbes and dietary antigens. The follicle-associated epithelium (FAE) is traditionally recognized by the presence of microfold cells (M cells) that mediate antigen sampling in PPs. By analyzing Gfi1b-eGFP reporter mice and human PP biopsies, we identified tuft cells as an additional, evolutionarily conserved FAE population that regulates mucosal immunity. Using mouse models and intestinal organoids, we demonstrate that M cells and tuft cells are distinct lineages arising from Pou2f3+ progenitors, whose differentiation is reciprocally regulated by RANKL and interleukin-13 (IL-13), respectively. Tuft cell-derived IL-25 activates type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) in PPs. Furthermore, IL-13 production by ILC2 enhances immunoglobulin A class switching and antigen-specific immunity. These findings reveal a dual surveillance system in the FAE, where developmentally related epithelial lineages use distinct mechanisms to coordinate mucosal immunity.

record.abstract: Recent advances in immune checkpoint blockade, chemotherapy, anti-angiogenic therapy, and molecularly targeted therapies have expanded therapeutic options for gastric cancer. However, primary and acquired resistance remain major barriers to achieving durable clinical benefit. Tumor cell-intrinsic molecular features, including HER2 status, PD-L1 expression, MSI/MMR status, claudin 18 isoform 2 (CLDN18.2), and fibroblast growth factor receptor 2b (FGFR2b) alterations, do not fully account for the substantial heterogeneity in treatment response, highlighting the need to consider the spatial organization of the tumor microenvironment. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are key components of this microenvironment. Evidence from single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, multiplex imaging, clinicopathological cohorts, and functional experiments indicates that CAFs and TAMs can form spatially organized niches through chemokine-mediated monocyte recruitment, macrophage-state reprogramming, extracellular matrix remodeling, complement signaling, cytokine networks, and immunometabolic regulation. Our synthesis identifies recurrent gastric cancer-associated niche archetypes, including CCL2⁺ fibroblast-STAT3-activated macrophage, GREM1⁺ fibroblast-SPP1⁺ macrophage, FAP⁺ fibroblast-SPP1⁺ macrophage, and THBS2⁺ matrix CAF-SPP1⁺ TAM niches. Among these, the THBS2⁺ matrix CAF-SPP1⁺ TAM niche in peritoneal metastasis has particularly strong spatial and functional support, including experimental evidence that CAF-derived C3 promotes C3AR1-dependent accumulation of SPP1⁺ TAMs and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. Other proposed interactions are supported to varying degrees by spatial colocalization, ligand-receptor inference, clinicopathological association, or experimental perturbation, but their causal and clinical relevance remains incompletely established. Collectively, the available evidence suggests that selected CAF-TAM niches may promote CD8⁺ T-cell exclusion, vascular dysfunction, impaired therapeutic delivery, and persistence of treatment-resistant tumor cells. Actionable pathways include CCL2-CCR2, CSF1-CSF1R, IL-6-JAK-STAT3, CXCL12-CXCR4, SPP1-integrin, FAP, TGF-β, LOX, and C3-C3AR1. Future strategies should move beyond non-selective depletion of CAFs or macrophages and instead integrate molecular subtype, metastatic site, treatment context, and spatial biomarker patterns to identify and selectively disrupt dominant pathogenic niches.

record.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic low-grade inflammation and immunosenescence accompany ageing and chronic disease. Exercise and physical activity are proposed to modify circulating inflammatory biomarkers, but review-level evidence is dispersed across populations and conditions.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and SPORTDiscus through 1 March 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and overviews on exercise or physical activity and circulating inflammaging- or immunosenescence-related biomarkers in older adults and adults with chronic diseases. We reported the review in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and PRIOR. Methodological quality was appraised with A MeaSurement Tool to Assess systematic Reviews, version 2 (AMSTAR-2), primary-study overlap with the corrected covered area, and certainty with GRADE. We performed no de novo meta-analysis or meta-regression; this umbrella review is a structured narrative synthesis of quantitative review-level estimates rather than a quantitative reanalysis.
RESULTS: Twenty-one reviews were included: 14 core-eligible (full Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes, and Study design [PICOS] match, contributing to the primary synthesis and conclusions) and seven evidence-map-only (partial PICOS match, used only for mapping and background). Among core-eligible reviews reporting standardised mean differences, exercise was associated with small reductions in tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha; point estimates - 1.42 to - 0.05, two of five confidence intervals excluding the null) and C-reactive protein (CRP; - 0.65 to - 0.47, two of three excluding the null), whereas interleukin-6 (IL-6) estimates were inconsistent (- 0.81 to + 0.09, two of five excluding the null). Heterogeneity was frequently high (I 2 up to 94%). Overall primary-study overlap was slight (corrected covered area [CCA] = 0.0091), but very high within the multiple sclerosis cluster (CCA = 0.4048). AMSTAR-2 confidence was critically low in 11 reviews, low in nine, and moderate in one; GRADE certainty was very low for every biomarker construct. A post hoc restricted descriptive sensitivity analysis excluding critically low reviews attenuated the apparent signal.
CONCLUSION: Exercise and physical activity may produce small reductions in some circulating inflammatory biomarkers, most consistently TNF-alpha and CRP, but effects on IL-6 are inconsistent, and certainty is very low. Effects on immunosenescence and cellular-senescence markers remain an evidence gap. This biomarker evidence alone is insufficient to justify prescribing exercise specifically to lower inflammatory biomarkers and does not alter broader physical-activity recommendations based on clinical and functional outcomes.PROSPERO: CRD420261410061.

record.abstract: Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) is a persistent environmental contaminant associated with immunometabolic toxicity; however, its effects on the intestinal microenvironment remain incompletely understood. We integrated a murine PFOA exposure model with untargeted serum metabolomics, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize intestinal injury and explore microbiota-metabolite-immune relationships. PFOA exposure caused dose-dependent body weight loss, colon shortening, histopathological injury, disrupted epithelial junctional staining, and increased proinflammatory cytokine concentrations. It was also associated with restructuring of the gut microbiota and broad alterations in serum tryptophan-related metabolites, including a metabolomic feature putatively annotated as indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), whose normalized relative abundance was reduced. Single-cell analyses indicated remodeling of epithelial, T-cell, and fibroblast states, including enrichment of a T helper 1 (Th1)-like transcriptional program and altered fibroblast-associated inflammatory pathways. IPA supplementation partially ameliorated several PFOA-associated intestinal and inflammatory phenotypes but did not broadly normalize α-diversity, β-diversity, the relative abundance of Clostridium, or the fibroblast-associated markers examined. In polarized murine Th1 cells, IPA reduced JAK2 and STAT3 phosphorylation; this effect was partially attenuated by the AhR antagonist CH-223191, consistent with AhR-dependent restraint of JAK-STAT signaling. CellChat analysis further identified computationally inferred changes in selected CD44-associated ligand-receptor pairs between fibroblasts and Th1 cells. Collectively, these findings support a model in which PFOA-associated perturbation of microbial tryptophan metabolism and IPA-related signaling may contribute to epithelial and immune dysfunction.

record.abstract: As the global population ages, the incidence of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) has increased. Neurodegenerative diseases have complex pathogenesis and currently lack fundamental treatment methods. The gut-brain axis (GBA) participates in the pathogenesis of NDDs through bidirectional communication between the gut microbiota and the central nervous system (CNS). This review systematically introduces the pathogenic characteristics of representative NDDs such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and multiple sclerosis (MS), as well as the association mechanisms between these diseases and GBA. The pathogenic characteristics of NDDs are closely related to changes in the composition of the gut microbiota and differences in gut microbiota metabolites (such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), neurotransmitters, tryptophan metabolites, etc.). These changes influence the CNS through multiple pathways, including neuroendocrine, vagus nerve, and immune regulation, ultimately contributing to the onset and progression of the diseases. Furthermore, we have collected and summarized preclinical and clinical evidence from recent years regarding therapeutic interventions based on the GBA mechanism, including probiotics, prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). Nevertheless, major knowledge gaps remain, particularly regarding causality between gut microbiota changes and NDDs, the underlying molecular mechanisms, and the clinical efficacy of GBA-targeted therapies. This article aims to review the mechanisms of the interaction between the gut microbiota and the brain in neurodegenerative diseases, and based on the existing experimental evidence, provide theoretical basis and future development directions for future prevention and treatment strategies targeting GBA.

record.abstract: Heart failure (HF) is a complex clinical syndrome characterized by progressive cardiac remodelling, metabolic dysregulation, and high morbidity and mortality worldwide. Emerging evidence suggests that metabolic reprogramming plays a central role in HF progression, among which tryptophan (TRP) metabolism has attracted increasing attention due to its involvement in inflammation, immune regulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and gut microbiota imbalance. TRP is mainly metabolised through the kynurenine pathway (KP), serotonin pathway, and gut microbiota-derived indole pathway, generating a series of bioactive metabolites with distinct cardiovascular effects. Recent studies have demonstrated that abnormal activation of the indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO)-driven KP contributes to HF progression by promoting inflammatory activation, oxidative stress, myocardial fibrosis, and ventricular remodelling. In parallel, gut microbiota-derived TRP metabolites participate in the gut-heart axis and influence mitochondrial function, immune homeostasis, and cardiometabolic remodelling. In addition, TRP-related metabolites, particularly kynurenine (KYN) and the kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratio (KTR), exhibit promising potential as biomarkers for HF severity assessment and prognostic stratification. This review systematically summarizes the activation characteristics of TRP metabolic pathways in HF and discusses their mechanistic involvement in inflammation, immune regulation, gut microbiota dysbiosis, myocardial injury, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Furthermore, emerging therapeutic strategies targeting TRP metabolism are highlighted, including pharmacological modulation, microbiota-targeted interventions, exogenous metabolite supplementation, and exercise-based metabolic regulation. Collectively, TRP metabolism represents a promising metabolic hub integrating immune, inflammatory, and mitochondrial signaling networks in HF and may provide novel opportunities for precision diagnosis and targeted therapy.

record.abstract: Podocyte injury and loss are major pathological features of proteinuria and renal dysfunction. Growing evidence has highlighted the contribution of metabolic reprogramming and disrupted metabolic homeostasis to podocyte injury in glomerular disease. Under pathological conditions, alterations in the local microenvironment, including hyperglycemia, lipid overload, mechanical stress, and inflammatory stimuli, can trigger maladaptive metabolic responses in podocytes, characterized by disturbances in glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism. These metabolic alterations may be accompanied by disrupted ion homeostasis and crosstalk with innate immune signaling, collectively aggravating the structural and functional damage of podocytes. However, pharmacological options that specifically target metabolic abnormalities in podocytes are limited. Natural products, including traditional Chinese medicine prescriptions, have shown potential for mitigating podocyte injury because of their capacity to act on multiple targets and pathways. A range of natural products may preserve podocyte integrity by correcting mitochondrial dysfunction, reducing oxidative stress, modulating metabolic substrate utilization, restoring ion homeostasis, and attenuating inflammatory responses. This review examines metabolic reprogramming and homeostatic disturbances in podocytes, outlines the mechanisms underlying podocyte metabolic dysfunction, and summarizes how natural products mitigate podocyte injury in glomerular diseases, such as diabetic kidney disease and membranous nephropathy, thereby offering perspectives on metabolic mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets for podocyte-directed interventions.

record.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Atopic dermatitis (AD) involves interconnected disturbances in epidermal barrier function, immune regulation, microbial homeostasis, and neuroimmune itch. Natural products influence several of these processes, but their mechanistic and clinical evidence remains fragmented.
PURPOSE: To assess natural product-based interventions for AD within a polypharmacological framework and identify priorities for clinical translation.
STUDY DESIGN: Mechanism-driven systematic review with qualitative narrative synthesis.
METHODS: PubMed and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to March 2026. Eligible studies evaluated isolated natural compounds, characterized extracts or formulations, natural lipids, or microbe-derived interventions in patients with AD or validated experimental models. Evidence was synthesized by chemotype, pathological axis, molecular target or pathway, study design, and translational relevance.
RESULTS: A total of 156 original studies were retained. Reported effects clustered around epidermal differentiation and lipid homeostasis, inflammatory signaling, host-microbial interactions, and pruriceptive pathways. Preclinical studies provided mechanistic evidence for barrier-restorative, immunomodulatory, microbiome-related, and antipruritic effects involving multiple pathways. Clinical studies reported improvements in disease severity, barrier-related measures, pruritus, and quality of life, although findings varied across interventions and study designs. Direct target engagement, exposure-response relationships, and contributions of individual constituents in multicomponent preparations remained incompletely resolved.
CONCLUSION: Natural products provide a pharmacologically diverse basis for intervention across interconnected AD pathways. Current evidence supports therapeutic potential and multitarget activity, although polypharmacological synergy, comparative efficacy, and long-term safety require further validation. Clinical translation requires reproducible product characterization, direct mechanistic validation, pharmacokinetic assessment, human-relevant models, and well-designed clinical studies.

record.abstract: Advances in intensive care have improved survival from acute critical illness, leading to a growing population of patients with chronic critical illness (CCI), many of whom require prolonged organ support. This condition is associated with persistent catabolism, inflammation, and poor long-term outcomes. Understanding the metabolic alterations underlying this failure to recover may help identify targets for monitoring and intervention. This review synthesizes current clinical and translational evidence on metabolic dysregulation in CCI and discusses its implications for monitoring, nutritional strategies, and therapeutic interventions. We performed a narrative review informed by a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE followed by manual reference screening. Preclinical, translational and clinical studies addressing energy metabolism, mitochondrial function, autophagy, ketone metabolism, inflammation and recovery trajectories in critical illness were qualitatively synthesized. Available evidence suggests that patients with CCI exhibit persistent metabolic inflexibility, impaired transition from catabolism to anabolism, mitochondrial dysfunction, altered autophagy, and disturbances in substrate utilization, including reduced ketogenesis. These alterations, together with epigenetic and immunometabolic reprogramming, may contribute to muscle wasting, immune dysfunction, and delayed functional recovery, features consistent with the persistent inflammation, immunosuppression and catabolism syndrome (PICS). Much of the mechanistic evidence, however, derives from preclinical or acute-phase studies, and validation of these findings in patients with CCI remains limited. CCI may represent a state of impaired metabolic and cellular adaptation associated with persistent inflammation, organ dysfunction, and failed recovery from acute critical illness. Improved understanding of these mechanisms may support more individualized metabolic monitoring, nutritional support, and therapeutic strategies. Further prospective and translational studies are required to determine clinical relevance and guide targeted interventions.

record.abstract: Rapid global population ageing is accelerating the burden of cardiometabolic disease, and inflammageing-the chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that accompanies advancing age-has emerged as a shared pathological substrate linking cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and type 2 diabetes mellitus in older adults. Increasing evidence identifies the gut microbiota as an upstream driver of this process, forming a modifiable feedback loop with the intestinal barrier, the immune system, and cardiometabolic homeostasis. With advancing age, beneficial taxa such as Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii decline in abundance, whereas pro-inflammatory taxa expand; this dysbiosis compromises tight-junction integrity, producing the "leaky gut" phenotype and permitting translocation of lipopolysaccharide and other pathogen-associated molecular patterns into the portal circulation. The resulting metabolic endotoxaemia activates TLR4/NF-κB signalling and sustains systemic elevations of IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β, which converge on insulin resistance, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and vascular injury. Microbiota-derived metabolites further shape this trajectory: trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) has been implicated in the acceleration of atherosclerosis, foam-cell formation, and platelet reactivity-largely on the basis of rodent studies and observational human data-whereas short-chain fatty acids reinforce barrier function and induce regulatory T cells. This review systematically synthesises current mechanistic and clinical evidence on the gut microbiota-inflammageing axis and its contribution to cardiometabolic deterioration during ageing, and critically appraises dietary intervention strategies as the most direct and actionable entry point into this feedback loop. The Mediterranean, Green-Mediterranean, and plant-based dietary patterns, together with intermittent fasting, have been shown to remodel the gut microbiota, reduce systemic inflammatory tone, and improve cardiometabolic risk profiles. Key dietary components-fibre-derived short-chain fatty acids, polyphenols and their microbial metabolites, omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids together with specialised pro-resolving mediators, and age-appropriate protein intake-act through distinct but converging molecular mechanisms to preserve barrier integrity, restore immunometabolic balance, and support healthy vascular ageing. Emerging translational approaches, including precision nutrition guided by individual microbiome profiles, next-generation probiotics, prebiotics and postbiotics, and small-molecule inhibitors targeting TMAO biosynthesis, are also examined, alongside their current translational limitations-including the absence of standardised microbiome analytical pipelines, strain-specific heterogeneity of probiotic effects, and the lack of formal recommendations in current cardiovascular and diabetes guidelines. Safety considerations relevant to frail older adults-such as hypoglycaemia risk during intermittent fasting, bleeding risk with high-dose omega-3 supplementation, and rare bacteraemia associated with probiotic use in immunocompromised individuals-are also highlighted. Research gaps such as scarce long-term follow-up, under-representation of non-Western populations, and heterogeneity across ageing stages are discussed. By integrating mechanistic insight with translational evidence, this review provides a theoretical foundation for the development of individualised nutritional strategies aimed at extending cardiometabolic healthspan in older adults.
